review_note: Preserve effect sizes and conditions; remove course-vindication history and the assumption that all field notes record failure.

edits.before: This reading is here because of what week 2 was about to do with it. The asleep test wants a justification, and the actor–observer asymmetry is the obvious one lying around: of course a note about someone else drifts to character, that's a documented bias. It isn't, at the size the story implies, and a course that asks students to check claims has to check the one that would have been most convenient for it.
edits.after: Week 2 does not use a blanket actor–observer bias to justify the asleep test. The test is the course's own rule of thumb: a rule about an exchange can be tested in another exchange; a verdict about a person is harder to check.
edits.reason: Replace retrospective self-praise with the current rationale for the teaching tool.

edits.before: So the asleep test stays, labelled as the course's own rule of thumb, argued for on the grounds that a rule about an exchange is testable next week and a verdict about a person is not. And one piece of Malle does survive into the week, sharpened rather than discarded: the asymmetry was there for negative events. You write a field note when something didn't go smoothly. The single condition under which the effect appears is the condition your journal entries are written in.
edits.after: The result for negative events is relevant when a journal entry records a conflict or a failed exchange. It does not mean every entry needs to concern one, and negative events were not the only condition in which the review found an asymmetry.
edits.reason: Remove an invented requirement that all journal entries concern failure and the incorrect simplification to a single study condition.
